title: Probability

sections.label: A
sections.instruction: Check how likely the event is.
sections.explainer: A probability is a number from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). 1/2 is as likely as not.

design.purpose: Describe a chance as impossible, unlikely, as likely as not, likely or certain.
design.rationale: Probability starts as words on a scale from impossible to certain, matched to numbers from 0 to 1. Each bag has a different mix of red and blue, including none and all red, so every word is used. The explainer ties 1/2 to as likely as not.
misconceptions: Judging by the number of red marbles instead of the share of red marbles.
references: Common Core Standards Writing Team (2011), Progressions for Statistics and Probability, 6-8

design.purpose: Find the probability of an outcome when all outcomes are equally likely.
design.rationale: When all outcomes are equally likely, a probability is the number of matching outcomes over the total. Some bags have three colors and some items ask for not a color, so the student counts the matching outcomes each time instead of copying a number.
misconceptions: Writing the ratio of red to blue instead of red to all.
Counting only the named color for a not question.
references: Common Core Standards Writing Team (2011), Progressions for Statistics and Probability, 6-8

sections.label: C
sections.instruction: Use the probability to predict the number of times.

nodes.text: A spinner has 8 equal parts. 1 part is red. It is spun 128 times. About how many times will it land on red?

blank.label: A spinner has 8 equal parts. 1 part is red. It is spun 128 times. About how many times will it land on red?

nodes.text: A spinner has 3 equal parts. 1 part is red. It is spun 24 times. About how many times will it land on red?

blank.label: A spinner has 3 equal parts. 1 part is red. It is spun 24 times. About how many times will it land on red?

design.purpose: Predict about how often an outcome happens in many trials from its probability.
design.rationale: The student multiplies a probability by the number of trials to predict a count. The number of spins is a multiple of the spinner's parts, so the prediction is a whole number. The word about reminds the student that real results will vary.
misconceptions: Thinking the prediction must happen exactly.
Dividing the trials by the number of red parts instead of all the parts.
references: Common Core Standards Writing Team (2011), Progressions for Statistics and Probability, 6-8

sections.label: D
sections.instruction: Use the results to estimate. Show your work.

stem.text: A paper cup is tossed 60 times. It lands on its side 42 times.

prompt.text: Estimate the probability it lands on its side.

field.label: probability of landing on its side

prompt.text: About how many times would it land on its side in 200 tosses?

field.label: landings on side in 200

nodes.text: A spinner landed on blue 18 times in 40 spins. Predict about how many times it will land on blue in 100 spins.

field.label: blue in 100 spins

design.purpose: Estimate a probability from observed results, and use it to predict.
design.rationale: Results from a real experiment, such as tossing a paper cup, give a probability that no list of outcomes can. The student estimates it as a fraction of trials, then uses it to predict, as the standard asks. A cup is chosen because its outcomes are not equally likely.
misconceptions: Assuming each outcome has the same chance, such as 1/2 for landing on its side.
Using the count of 42 as the probability.
references: Common Core Standards Writing Team (2011), Progressions for Statistics and Probability, 6-8
